title: High-touch surfaces and risk-based frequencies
audience: Cleaners and cleaning supervisors who clean shared and resident areas in residential aged care, clinics, dental practices and NDIS settings in any Australian state or territory.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NHMRC, Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) (no page date shown; document dated 2019); NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4, Core Module (cover date November 2021; no page date shown).
learningOutcomes: Identify the high-touch surfaces in a care or clinical area and explain why they are prioritised.
Apply a facility cleaning frequency schedule and explain how risk changes it.
Recognise when a schedule change is needed and state who authorises it.
Record the frequency applied, the surfaces cleaned and any change requested.

instruction.heading: What a high-touch surface is
instruction.body: A high-touch surface is one that many people touch with their hands, often in quick succession. Examples in a care or clinical setting include door handles, handrails, call bell buttons, light switches, bed rails and tables, taps and sink handles, toilet flush levers, commode lids, lift buttons, shared phones and keyboards, and trolley handles. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (document dated 2019) recommend cleaning frequently touched surfaces with detergent solution at least daily and when visibly soiled. The NDIS Practice Standards, Version 4 of November 2021, require routine environmental cleaning in settings other than participants' homes, with particular attention to frequently touched surfaces. The list of surfaces and the frequency for each are set by the facility's risk assessment.

instruction.heading: Risk-based frequency
instruction.body: Frequency is decided by risk, not by convenience. A handrail in a busy corridor used by many residents and visitors needs more frequent cleaning than a wall in a storeroom. A bathroom used by several residents in one day needs more attention than a single room used by one resident. The facility's schedule records these decisions, and it may set a higher frequency for a unit with known risks or after an event. Your job is to apply the frequency on the schedule, and to recognise when the actual use of an area has changed so that the schedule may no longer match the risk.

instruction.heading: Mapping the surfaces in your area
instruction.body: Before you start an area, walk it and list the high-touch surfaces it contains. Compare that list to the facility schedule. If a surface is missing from the schedule, or a surface on the schedule is no longer used, note the difference and tell your supervisor. Do not add or remove surfaces from the schedule yourself. In a resident room, check bed rails, call bells, bedside tables, the bathroom door, and any shared equipment that is part of the room's approved list, and leave clinical devices to the clinical team.

instruction.heading: When a change is needed
instruction.body: A schedule may need to change when an outbreak is declared, when a resident's needs change, when a new piece of equipment arrives, or when an inspection finds a gap. A change to frequency or to the list of surfaces must be authorised by the person responsible for the schedule, usually the IPC lead or the facility manager, and it must be confirmed in writing. Until the change is confirmed, follow the current schedule and report the concern. A change that is suggested by a resident or family member is passed on for review, and it is not applied directly.

instruction.heading: Worked scenario: the handrail that is touched all day
instruction.body: A resident repeatedly touches a handrail that several other residents also use, while the schedule lists only end-of-day cleaning for the handrail. You notice the handrail looks used several times in the morning. The appropriate response is to follow the schedule as written, tell the supervisor what you observed, and ask for the frequency to be reviewed. Record the observation, the time and the person told. Do not increase the frequency yourself, and do not clean the handrail in a way that is not approved.

procedure: Walk the area and list the high-touch surfaces, comparing the list to the facility schedule.
Apply the frequency on the schedule for each surface, using the approved product and method.
Note any surface missing from the schedule, or any change in use, and tell the supervisor.
Do not change the frequency or the list of surfaces yourself. Wait for written authorisation.
Record the surfaces cleaned, the frequency applied, the product used and any concern raised, with the time.

workedExamples.situation: The schedule lists a bathroom door handle for cleaning only at the end of the day. You see that the handle is touched by several residents throughout the morning and is visibly soiled.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do about the handle?
workedExamples.reasoning: Clean the handle now, because it is visibly soiled, using the approved product. Record that you cleaned it outside the scheduled time, and why. Tell the supervisor that the schedule may not reflect the use of the handle, and ask for the frequency to be reviewed. Do not change the schedule yourself.

workedExamples.situation: A new call bell system has been installed in a unit, and the schedule does not list the new buttons.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you add them to your round?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not add them unless the schedule or a written instruction includes them. Tell the supervisor that the new buttons are not on the schedule and ask for a written decision. Record the concern and the time.

commonErrors.error: Cleaning only the surfaces that look dirty and missing others that are touched often.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the high-touch list and the schedule. Clean the listed surfaces whether or not they look soiled.

commonErrors.error: Changing the frequency on the schedule without written authority.
commonErrors.prevention: Frequency changes are authorised in writing by the responsible person. Report the concern and wait.

commonErrors.error: Assuming that a surface is not high-touch because it is not on the list.
commonErrors.prevention: Walk the area and report any surface that is clearly touched often but is missing from the schedule.

commonErrors.error: Cleaning clinical equipment as part of a surfaces round.
commonErrors.prevention: Clinical devices are left to the clinical team unless the facility authorises the task in writing.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) recommend cleaning frequently touched surfaces with detergent solution at least daily and when visibly soiled, and cleaning shared clinical equipment between patient uses.

The NDIS Practice Standards, Version 4 of November 2021, Core Module, require routine environmental cleaning in settings other than participants' homes, with particular attention to frequently touched surfaces.
The frequency for each surface in residential aged care is taken from the facility's risk assessment and infection prevention plan (the NDIS text read does not state a frequency).

Licence notice: Applying a facility schedule does not grant any authority to change the schedule, set infection prevention precautions, or make risk decisions for residents. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority.

qualityStandard: The learner lists the high-touch surfaces in a supplied area and compares the list to a supplied schedule, identifying one gap.
The learner applies the scheduled frequency to a supplied surface list with the correct product and method.
The learner raises a schedule concern in writing or to the supervisor without changing the schedule.
The learner records the surfaces cleaned, the frequency applied and any concern raised.
documentationEvidence: Surfaces cleaned, the frequency applied, the product used and the time
Any gap identified between the schedule and the area, and the supervisor told
Any out-of-schedule clean, with the reason
summary: High-touch surfaces are cleaned at the frequency the facility sets from its risk assessment.
Frequency and the surface list are changed only by written authority from the responsible person.
Report a gap or a change in use; do not change the schedule yourself.
Record the surfaces, the frequency, the product and any concern.

knowledgeChecks.question: What decides how often a high-touch surface is cleaned?
options: How clean the surface looks at the start of the shift.
The facility's risk assessment, reflected in its schedule.
The cleaner's own judgement of how often it is needed.

knowledgeChecks.question: A surface you touch often is missing from the schedule. What should you do?
options: Add it to your round and clean it at the end of the shift.
Ignore it, because it is not on the schedule.
Tell the supervisor, and do not change the schedule yourself.

knowledgeChecks.question: Who authorises a change to cleaning frequency?
options: The person responsible for the schedule, in writing, usually the IPC lead or facility manager.
Any cleaner on the unit, if they think it is needed, since they see the room every day
A family member who has asked for more cleaning in the room during the visit
